air_research.image_alt: Illustration of an unoccupied bedroom overlooking a city at dusk
air_research.publication: Research from Cambridge, Tsinghua & Sleep Cycle
air_research.heading: What Happens In The Air Shows Up At Night.
air_research.detail_heading: The Link Between Air Pollution And Nighttime Coughing.
air_research.intro: A study spanning 32 cities linked higher levels of outdoor fine-particle pollution with more frequent coughing at night.
air_research.finding_context: Associated with each 10 µg/m³ increase in outdoor PM₂.₅ concentration.
air_research.scope: 32 cities across 12 countries. Approximately 500 days of observations.
air_research.method_intro: Researchers combined city-level air measurements with anonymized cough counts from Sleep Cycle, then tested whether daily changes were related.
air_research.method_air_text: Monitoring stations supplied daily concentrations of PM₂.₅ for each city.
air_research.method_cough_text: The app detected coughing during sleep recordings. Researchers calculated coughs per recorded hour and grouped the data by city and day.
air_research.method_compare_text: Statistical models accounted for weather and influenza activity. City-level results were combined to estimate the overall association.
air_research.particles_text: PM₂.₅ refers to fine airborne particles no more than 2.5 micrometres in diameter. The study examined outdoor concentrations, rather than measuring the air beside each participant’s bed.
air_research.lower_heading: The Link Extended To Lower Pollution Levels.
air_research.lower_text: The researchers also detected associations below the WHO’s 24-hour PM₂.₅ guideline. The findings suggest nighttime coughing can respond to changes in air pollution even at relatively low concentrations.
air_research.limits_heading: What The Findings Can Tell Us
air_research.limits_text: This observational study identifies an association; it does not establish cause and effect. Outdoor monitoring cannot capture each person’s indoor exposure, which varies with ventilation, buildings and filtration.
air_research.product_limit: The study did not test AirTulip or measure whether an air purifier improves sleep. Its findings provide context for air-quality research, not evidence of a product’s clinical benefit.
air_research.estimate_text: The combined city-specific estimate was a relative risk of 1.024 per 10 µg/m³ increase in PM₂.₅ (95% confidence interval: 1.013–1.035). This corresponds to an estimated 2.4% increase in cough frequency, with a confidence interval of 1.3%–3.5%. It is a population-level estimate, not a prediction for an individual.
air_research.short_limit: Observational research on outdoor pollution and coughing. The study did not test AirTulip or improvements in sleep quality.
air_research.citation: Xia et al. Short-term associations between air pollution and nocturnal cough frequency. Communications Health, 15 September 2026.
air_research.cambridge_citation: University of Cambridge. Sleep app tracks link between air pollution and a bad night’s sleep. 15 September 2026.

air_science.label: The Science Behind AirTulip
air_science.hero_title: Cleaner Air Starts Where You Breathe.
air_science.hero_text: A filter captures particles. Airflow determines where the filtered air goes. AirTulip brings those two ideas together at the head of your bed.
air_science.airflow_alt: Green laser light reveals airflow above a person reclining against an AirTulip headboard
air_science.airflow_caption: AirTulip airflow demonstration, made visible with laser light and airborne particles.
air_science.flow_text: The breathing zone is the air immediately around your nose and mouth. It is the point where room air becomes the air you inhale.
air_science.flow_detail: AirTulip Sleep is designed to deliver filtered air directly toward this area. The headboard combines filtration with a broad, directed outlet, rather than relying only on air mixing throughout the bedroom.
air_science.step_1_text: Room air passes through the headboard's particle filters before it reaches the outlet.
air_science.step_2_text: Internal channels guide the filtered air into an organized stream. This controlled delivery is the principle behind AirTulip's laminar airflow design.
air_science.step_3_text: The outlet sits at the head of the bed, close to the sleeper's breathing zone. Placement and airflow work together.
air_science.filter_alt: Two pleated AirTulip Sleep particle filters
air_science.filter_title: Filtration Is Only Part Of The Design.
air_science.filter_text: The pleats give the filter a large surface area in a compact space. AirTulip's engineering also considers the fan, internal air channels and the shape of the outlet.
air_science.filter_detail: Filter efficiency describes what happens as air passes through a filter. It does not, by itself, describe the concentration of particles at your pillow. That depends on the complete system and the conditions around it.
air_science.lab_title: Make The Air Visible. Then Measure It.
air_science.lab_text: Airflow is invisible in everyday use. Visualization and instruments let engineers examine how it travels and where to take measurements.
air_science.lab_alt: AirTulip headboard with instruments and sensors in an Eindhoven University of Technology laboratory
air_science.lab_caption: AirTulip laboratory setup at Eindhoven University of Technology, from the AirTulip engineering archive.
air_science.measure_1_text: Laser light makes suspended particles visible, revealing the movement of air. The demonstration shows flow behavior; it is not a numerical filtration test.
air_science.measure_2_text: A measurement beside the sleeper answers a different question from a room average. Sensor location and test conditions matter when interpreting a result.
air_science.measure_3_text: Air delivery, filtration and acoustic design must work together in a headboard intended for overnight use. The engineering process includes prototypes, test rigs and airflow modeling.
air_science.university_title: Why Air Delivery Deserves Its Own Research.
air_science.university_text: Research into personalized ventilation asks a precise question: can delivering air close to a person change the air they inhale?
air_science.university_method: Appendix H of Hailin Zheng's doctoral thesis describes preliminary climate-chamber experiments using an AirTulip-supplied ventilation interface. Researchers varied the direction and rate of air supply around a breathing and thermal model in a semi-enclosed baby bed. Head-side delivery produced the lowest inhaled CO₂ concentration among the tested directions at 55 m³/h.
air_science.university_limit: This was a model-based ventilation experiment, not a clinical trial of AirTulip Sleep. CO₂ served as a measure of ventilation performance. The findings do not establish that a recirculating headboard removes CO₂, improves sleep or is suitable for infant use.
air_science.use_title: From The Laboratory To The Bedroom.
air_science.use_text: The practical idea is simple: bring filtered air close to a person who stays in one place. The bedroom gives that idea a clear purpose.
air_science.bedroom_title: At The Head Of Your Bed
air_science.bedroom_text: AirTulip Sleep incorporates the airflow system into the headboard. It puts the outlet near the pillow without adding a separate tower beside the bed.
air_science.routine_text: Keep the air path unobstructed and maintain the filters as directed. Filtration works alongside source control and appropriate ventilation; it does not replace either.
air_science.office_alt: An earlier AirTulip tower installed in a shared office lounge
air_science.office_text: An AirTulip tower in an office lounge. Earlier installations explored air delivery around people seated in a shared space.
air_science.dental_alt: An earlier AirTulip tower beside a dental treatment chair
air_science.dental_text: An AirTulip tower beside a dental chair, showing another setting where a person remains in a defined position.
air_science.archive_note: Installation photographs from AirTulip's archive show earlier systems, not the current Sleep headboard. They document applications, not clinical outcomes or infection-prevention effectiveness.
air_science.faq_title: A Closer Look At The Evidence.
air_science.faq_text: The distinction between a mechanism, a laboratory result and a health outcome matters.
air_science.question_1: Did The Cambridge Study Test AirTulip?
air_science.answer_1: No. It examined the association between outdoor fine-particle pollution and nighttime coughing recorded by a sleep app. It did not test an air purifier or establish a sleep benefit from AirTulip.
air_science.question_2: Does A Laser Demonstration Prove Particle Removal?
air_science.answer_2: It makes airflow and suspended particles visible. A quantified removal claim also needs particle measurements, a documented protocol and clearly stated operating conditions.
air_science.question_3: Is This A Substitute For Ventilation?
air_science.answer_3: No. Particle filtration and ventilation do different jobs. Ventilation exchanges indoor and outdoor air; a recirculating particle filter does not remove the CO₂ people exhale.
air_science.question_4: Does The University Research Prove Better Sleep?
air_science.answer_4: No. The cited thesis experiment measured ventilation around a breathing model. It did not measure sleep quality or clinical health outcomes in people using AirTulip Sleep.
air_science.end_title: See The Engineering In Your Bedroom.
air_science.end_text: Explore the headboard, its design and the details of everyday use.
